extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and platform designers interested in online media and journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing and understanding clickbait: its defining characteristics (how headlines/teasers misrepresent or withhold information), common tactics, aims (drive clicks/ads), harms (misinformation/phishing), and platform detection/mitigation approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation in the enticement
rubrics_metrics.description: A defining characteristic of clickbait is misrepresentation in the enticement presented to the user to manipulate them to click onto a link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly emphasises that clickbait 'is designed to attract attention and to entice users to follow' links and is 'typically deceptive, sensationalized, or otherwise misleading.' Use this as a primary criterion: does the headline/teaser present the content honestly or does it misrepresent what the click-through contains?

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation of the 'curiosity gap' (teaser)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'teaser' aims to exploit the 'curiosity gap', providing just enough information to make readers curious, but not enough to satisfy without clicking through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines that purposefully withhold key information to create suspense or an information gap (e.g., 'You won't believe what happened next') fit this criterion. The presence of a deliberate information gap is diagnostic of clickbait tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overpromises and underdelivers
rubrics_metrics.description: A more commonly used definition is a headline that intentionally overpromises and underdelivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the headline's claim is stronger or more sensational than the article's content. BuzzFeed's operational definition (dishonesty about content) is aligned with this: eye-catching phrasing alone is not clickbait if it accurately describes the content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism and exaggeration (yellow journalism lineage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clickbait techniques are derivative of yellow journalism: eye-catching headlines that include exaggerations, scandal-mongering, or sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for sensational language or framing that prioritizes shock/novelty over accurate reporting. Historical analogy to yellow journalism indicates similar ethical concerns around accuracy and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline accuracy versus mere attention-grabbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'eye-catching' is not necessarily clickbait if the headline 'accurately described the article'—the distinction is whether the headline is dishonest about content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accuracy as a differentiator: publications (e.g., BuzzFeed per article) may write eye-catching headlines that are acceptable provided they deliver what they promise; dishonest mismatch constitutes clickbait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unoriginal or low-value content (content farms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The articles associated with such headlines often are unoriginal, and either merely restate the headline, or copy content from a more genuine news source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess content quality: if the article adds little beyond the headline, or repackages existing work without value, it meets a common clickbait pattern (content farm style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion/greed/prurient-interest triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Clickbait exploits curiosity related to greed or prurient interest and frequently uses emotional subjects with stark headlines that are widely shared and clicked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the headline is engineered to provoke strong emotions (outrage, disgust, prurience) or promises gains (get-rich schemes). Such triggers are typical tactics to inflate click-through rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lewd imagery or 'make money quick' schemes as enticement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not uncommon for clickbait contents to include lewd imagery or a 'make money quick' scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visuals and promises of easy money are concrete signals of low-quality, attention-focused content and may indicate malicious or exploitative intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use to drive page views / advertising revenue (CTR optimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clickbait is primarily used to drive page views on websites, whether to increase online advertising revenue or to optimize a creator's overall engagement; clickbait tactics generally lead to higher clickthrough rates (CTRs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate intent and metrics focus: if headline choices are clearly optimized for CTR/ad revenue rather than information value, they conform to clickbait practices. Platforms and creators may prioritize CTR even if content quality is low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement bait (manipulative interaction solicitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement bait is manipulative content that is designed to elicit users into interaction (comments, likes, shares, tags) and is used in social media marketing to artificially inflate interactions for monetization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate from simple curiosity-driven clickbait, engagement bait explicitly requests or gamifies user interaction (e.g., 'Like if... Share if...'). Platforms treat this as a distinct harmful pattern and often demote it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in phishing and malware distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Clickbait can be used for phishing attacks for the purpose of spreading malicious files or stealing user information; the attack occurs once the user opens the link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sensational or misleading links as potential security threats, not only low-quality journalism. Presence of downloads, suspicious redirects, or requests for credentials after click-through are red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline composition techniques (suspense, thumbnails, numbered lists, chumboxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular approaches include composing headlines that build suspense and sensation, presenting interesting link images/thumbnails, and promising easy-to-read numbered lists; chumbox-style adverts employ common clickbait tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize structural devices (listicles, 'Top N', dramatic thumbnails) commonly used to increase shareability and clicks. These devices are not inherently clickbait unless combined with misrepresentation or low-value content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-detection signals and mitigation (time-on-page, algorithms, filters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms like Facebook use cues such as time spent on the linked page to distinguish clickbait from non-clickbait; social media platforms and browsers have implemented algorithms and tools to filter or detect clickbait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detection approaches include measuring dwell time, CTR vs. engagement quality, and supervised learning (reporting plug-ins). These operational signals are used to algorithmically demote or filter clickbait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backlash and ethical evaluation (undermining accuracy/veracity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chasing down cheap clicks at the expense of accuracy and veracity undermines the value of journalism and truth, prompting backlash (e.g., satirical responses like ClickHole and platform policy changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate clickbait not only technically but ethically: does the practice erode trust, promote misinformation, or harm public discourse? Ethical harms are a core evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform definition variation (e.g., Facebook vs Merriam‑Webster vs publishers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different actors define clickbait differently: Merriam‑Webster focuses on 'designed to make readers want to click' (especially for dubious value), Dictionary.com highlights sensationalized headlines, Facebook defines it as a headline that encourages clicks but 'does not tell them what they will see', while some publishers (e.g., BuzzFeed editorial) restrict the term to dishonest headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying content, be explicit about which operational definition you are using—platform enforcement definitions may differ from colloquial or dictionary definitions, affecting what is labelled clickbait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic amplification and recommendation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Streaming platforms' recommendations and personalization (e.g., YouTube) can amplify clickbait because videos with hyperbolic or misleading titles showed higher CTRs and recommendations prioritize high-click content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for systemic effects: a headline may be incentivized by recommendation algorithms, and assessment should consider how platform mechanics (personalization, recommendation ranking) interact with clickbait incentives.
